green.label: Pro, with conditions
green.short: Supports AI / data centers AND says they must pay their own way or leave the community better off (own power, no ratepayer subsidy, local benefits, local say).

yellow.label: Mixed / unclear
yellow.short: Wishy-washy, contradictory, or only partly formed: e.g. states conditions but also backs incentives, or opposes one project without saying what would be acceptable.

orange.label: Opposed, no nuance
orange.short: Opposes data centers or backs pauses/moratoria without describing terms under which one would be welcome.

red.label: Pro, no nuance
red.short: Backs AI / data-center growth (incentives, speed) with no stated protections for ratepayers or the host community.

gray.label: No position found
gray.short: No public statement found as of the update date, or the office (judge, clerk, sheriff) does not set AI / data-center policy. Not a rating.

cands.bio: Former NC governor (2017-2024) and attorney general.
cands.rec: As governor he celebrated large tech and data-center investments that received state incentives; the NRSC calls his 2026 stance a flip-flop (partisan source).

ai.why: Accepts data centers but says they must pay for all of their power, should build their own generation, and that local communities get the final say (including local moratoriums). Has not called for a ban.
ai.q: We need to make sure data centers pay for their own power and we need to encourage them to build their own energy sources because right now that's causing rates to go up for consumers.

cands.bio: Former Republican National Committee chair and former NC GOP chair.
cands.rec: NC Democrats, citing his family financial disclosure, say he holds up to $1.6M in data-center company investments and at least $149K of Duke Energy stock (claims made at a Democratic press event; check the disclosure yourself).

ai.why: Strong pay-your-own-way terms (Big Tech buys every megawatt and every grid upgrade, zero cost to households, communities decide) would read green, BUT he also backs tax breaks for data centers (fails your "no subsidy" test) and told Fox News local opposition "is not organic" and is "being ginned up". ai.q: We don't want to lose the AI race to China ... but you can't have the data centers be a burden to local communities.

cands.bio: State representative since 2019.
cands.rec: Co-sponsor of HB 1063 (2026), the House Democrats' data-center bill.

ai.why: Inferred from co-sponsoring HB 1063, which lets data centers build but makes them pay their own way: report power and water use, big ones (over 40 MW or 1 billion liters of water a year) must self-supply at least 25% carbon-free power, repeal their state sales-tax breaks, and ban ratepayer-funded and local tax incentives. That is close to your green example. No personal statement found.
ai.q: (Lead sponsor Rep. Lindsey Prather, not Dahle) If a company wants to build a data center in North Carolina, they can. They must simply pay their own way.

referenda.title: Require photo ID for all voting
referenda.text: Extends the constitution's photo-ID requirement from in-person voting to every method of voting, including absentee by mail.

referenda.title: Cap the state income tax at 3.5%
referenda.text: Lowers the constitutional ceiling on state personal and corporate income tax rates from 7% to 3.5%.

referenda.title: Limit local property-tax increases
referenda.text: Requires the General Assembly to pass laws limiting property-tax levy increases by local governments; the actual limit would be set by later legislation.

context.t: New Hill (south Wake) 300 MW data-center proposal withdrawn after heavy opposition; Apex later adopts a one-year moratorium.
NC House Democrats file HB 1063 (disclosure, 25% clean self-supply for large sites, repeal tax breaks). Gov. Stein urges a review of data-center tax breaks.

NC House passes GOP SB 730 "Ratepayer Protection Act" 69-44 (data centers must cover their own grid costs, no local incentives or eminent domain, plus nuclear/coal provisions Democrats opposed). It has sat in Senate Rules since.
Holly Springs adopts a one-year pause on data centers.
Cary Town Council unanimously adopts an 18-month data-center moratorium (through Feb 2028) to study power, water, noise and siting. No applications were pending.
Southeast Raleigh data-center annexation withdrawn; Wake County itself has not considered a moratorium.
AG Jeff Jackson asks regulators for a separate Duke Energy rate class for data centers.
U.S. House passes the federal Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3 (large data centers cover grid and generation costs).
Raleigh City Council scheduled to vote on a six-month moratorium.
